# Week 4, Day 5.2 — Testing what a page looks like

Every assertion so far checked *text, URLs or counts*. None would notice if the login button turned
bright orange, moved 200 pixels left, or vanished behind a banner.

By the end of this lesson Playwright compares screenshots pixel by pixel — and you'll know why this
is the most abandoned kind of test in the industry.

> **Mode: test-runner, own config.** Two reasons the visual spec doesn't join the default suite: on the
> first run there is **no baseline**, so it fails by design while creating one; and baselines are
> **platform-specific**. A default suite that goes red on a clean checkout is useless, so this lives
> under `week4/generated/day5-visual.config.ts`.

## How it works: baseline, actual, diff

| Run | What happens |
|---|---|
| **1st** | no baseline exists → **test fails**, and the screenshot is saved as the baseline |
| **2nd+** | compares against that file; identical → pass |
| after a real UI change | fails, and writes **expected / actual / diff** images |

That first row surprises everyone. A failing first run is not a bug — it's the tool asking you to
confirm the baseline is what you wanted.

**Where it goes:** a folder next to the spec named `<spec-filename>-snapshots/`.

## The filename carries the platform

The baselines this lesson generated, verbatim:

```
day5-visual.visualdemo.ts-snapshots/table1-only-win32.png
day5-visual.visualdemo.ts-snapshots/tables-masked-win32.png
day5-visual.visualdemo.ts-snapshots/tables-page-win32.png
```

**`-win32`.** Playwright stamps the platform in because fonts and rendering genuinely differ between
Windows, macOS and Linux. With **named** projects the browser name joins it too (`-chromium-win32`).

The consequence: **a baseline captured on your laptop will fail in CI** if CI runs a different OS.
Teams solve that by generating baselines inside the same container CI uses.
## Example 1 — the spec, and the two-run dance

> ▶ **Run it yourself:**
> ```
> npx playwright test -c week4/generated/day5-visual.config.ts
> npx playwright test -c week4/generated/day5-visual.config.ts --update-snapshots
> ```

**Expected:** `4 passed` — because the baselines are committed. Delete the `-snapshots` folder and the
first run reports **3 failed, 1 passed**. (The one that still passes is Step 4; the next section
explains why.)

## Four things that make it survivable

The demo uses all four. Without them visual tests fail constantly for reasons that have nothing to do
with your application.

| Setting | Stops |
|---|---|
| a fixed `viewport` | a different window size producing different pixels |
| `animations: "disabled"` | catching a CSS transition mid-flight |
| `caret: "hide"` | a blinking cursor present in one shot, absent in the next |
| `maxDiffPixelRatio: 0.01` | anti-aliasing and font smoothing counting as a change |

That last one is a judgement call: too tight and every run is red, too loose and a real regression
slips through. 1% is a reasonable start for a page; tighten it for a single element.

**Prefer one element over a whole page.** `expect(page.locator("#table1")).toHaveScreenshot()` can only
be broken by that table. A full-page shot can be broken by anything — a cookie banner, an advert, a
date.
## Example 2 — a screenshot is not an assertion

**Expected:** two byte counts, the full page larger.

`page.screenshot({ path })` saves evidence. Useful when a developer asks *"what did it look like?"* —
and **worthless as a test**, because nothing is checked and nothing can fail.

| Want | Use |
|---|---|
| a test that fails when the UI changes | `expect(...).toHaveScreenshot()` |
| an image in the HTML report | `testInfo.attach(...)` |
| an image on failure only | config `screenshot: "only-on-failure"` |

That last row is the one to reach for — the config already does it for every test, so you almost never
need `page.screenshot()` by hand. Which is exactly the conclusion the session reached out loud.

// Your turn — retype the example above from memory, then run it.
// Typing beats reading. Peek above if you get stuck.

## Best practices

- **Static pages only.** Anything with a clock, carousel or live data will never settle.
- **Element over full page.**
- **Fix the viewport**, disable animations, hide the caret.
- **Generate baselines where CI runs them.**
- **Review a diff before `--update-snapshots`.**
- **Baseline the pages users see most** — a checkout, a dashboard. Not every screen.

## Common mistakes

| You see | Usually means | Fix |
|---|---|---|
| First run fails | no baseline yet — by design | run again, and review the image |
| Passes locally, fails in CI | different OS → different pixels | baseline in CI's container |
| Fails every run by a few pixels | anti-aliasing | small `maxDiffPixelRatio` |
| Fails after an intended redesign | stale baseline | review the diff, then `--update-snapshots` |
| Screenshot test never fails | you used `page.screenshot()` | that saves; `toHaveScreenshot()` asserts |
| Random failures on one region | dynamic content | `mask: [locator]` |

**Next:** [Day 5.3](/learn/w4/d5/p3) — when visual testing is worth it.

parts.title: When visual testing is worth it

blocks.text:
# Week 4, Day 5.3 — When visual testing is worth it

Same assertion as [Day 5.2](/learn/w4/d5/p2). No new API. The question is whether to use it at all —
because visual tests are abandoned more often than any other kind.

## Why they get abandoned

A visual test fails when **any** pixel changes. Most pixel changes are not bugs:

| Change | A bug? |
|---|---|
| the Submit button turned orange | maybe — ask the designer |
| a font rendered 1px differently after an OS update | no |
| an advert rotated | no |
| the header moved 200px because a CSS file failed to load | **yes** |
| a timestamp advanced by a second | no |

Four of five are noise. A suite that cries wolf four times out of five gets muted, then deleted.
Everything in Day 5.2's "survivable" table exists to shift that ratio.

## Determinism is the entry requirement — and it is measurable

Before baselining a page, check it renders the same twice. I ran that check on this course's banking
app:

```
shot 1 bytes: 31868   shot 2 bytes: 38418
byte-identical across 1.5s: false
```

**Two screenshots of the same page, 1.5 seconds apart, are different sizes.** Something loads or
animates late. A baseline from that page would fail unpredictably forever — and no
`maxDiffPixelRatio` fixes a page that hasn't finished rendering.

That's why Day 5.2 uses a deliberately static third-party page. Not a preference: the banking app
**fails the entry requirement**.

**Run this check first, on any page you're about to baseline.** Thirty seconds of work that saves weeks
of flaky failures.

**Expected:** the snippet, then the four options.

That last option is a real answer. Not every page should have a visual test, and choosing not to write
one is a decision rather than a failure.

## Where it genuinely pays

| Good candidate | Why |
|---|---|
| a checkout or payment page | a layout break costs money directly |
| a design-system component library | consistency *is* the requirement |
| a print or PDF export | no text assertion catches a layout break |
| an empty state or error page | rarely exercised, easy to break unnoticed |
| a page after a CSS framework upgrade | exactly what text assertions can't see |

| Poor candidate | Why |
|---|---|
| a dashboard with live numbers | never identical twice |
| a feed or search results | content changes by the minute |
| anything with adverts | not your pixels |
| a page you're actively redesigning | you'd re-baseline daily |

The pattern: **visual tests protect things that are supposed to stop changing.**

> This capability used to be expensive. Licensed tools called it a *bitmap checkpoint*. Getting it free
> in an open-source runner is genuinely new — which is also why teams adopt it before deciding where it
> belongs.

## What a reviewer checks

- **Was determinism checked** before the page was baselined?
- **Element or page?** A full-page baseline needs justifying.
- **Viewport pinned**, animations disabled.
- **Baselines generated in CI's environment**, not on a laptop.
- **Does the diff get reviewed**, or is `--update-snapshots` run reflexively?
- **Is the page one that should stop changing?**

**Next:** [Day 5.4](/learn/w4/d5/p4) — your turn.

# Week 4, Day 5.4 — Practice

Three problems. No answer key.

Config to copy: `week4/generated/day5-visual.config.ts`. Static page safe to baseline:
`https://the-internet.herokuapp.com/tables`.

> **Before you baseline anything**, run the determinism check from [Day 5.3](/learn/w4/d5/p3).

> Stuck past twenty minutes? Back to [Day 5.2](/learn/w4/d5/p2).

## When you're done

**Problem 3 is the one that matters.** Visual testing is easy to start and hard to keep. A test you had
to mask into meaninglessness is worse than no test — it costs maintenance and catches nothing, while
looking like coverage on a dashboard.

## Where week 4 landed

| Day | Built |
|---|---|
| [Day 1](/learn/w4/d1/p1) | debugging — headed, `slowMo`, `pause()`, Inspector, traces |
| [Day 2](/learn/w4/d2/p1) | elements you can't reach — frames, hover, right-click, drag |
| [Day 3](/learn/w4/d3/p1) | script- and test-level overrides |
| [Day 4](/learn/w4/d4/p1) | data-driven testing — JSON, Excel, CSV |
| Day 5 | visual regression, and when not to use it |

problems.statement:
**Build.** Walk the baseline lifecycle deliberately.

1. A visual test on one element of the tables page
2. Run it — record the result and find the file it created
3. Run it again — record the result
4. Delete the baseline and run a third time

**Check yourself.** Run 1 fails, run 2 passes, run 3 fails again. Note the exact filename and say what
its suffix tells you about where this baseline can and cannot be used.

> **Hint** — the suffix is the answer to "why did CI fail when it passes on my machine?"

**Build.** Make a visual test fail for a real reason, then decide what to do.

1. Baseline the `#table1` element
2. Change the page **before** the screenshot with `page.addStyleTag()` — alter a colour or size
3. Run it; open the HTML report and look at expected / actual / diff
4. Decide: bug or intended change? Act accordingly — fix the test, or re-baseline

**Check yourself.** You can describe what the diff showed, and you made a *decision* rather than
reflexively re-baselining. Write the one sentence you'd put in the pull request.

> **Hint** — `addStyleTag` simulates a developer's CSS change without touching a real site.

**Build.** Prove a page is unsuitable, then make it suitable.

1. Pick a page that is **not** deterministic — the course banking dashboard qualifies
2. Run the determinism check and record the evidence
3. Now make a visual test on it that **passes reliably ten times in a row**, using any combination of:
   a single stable element, `mask`, `animations: "disabled"`, waiting for a real condition
4. Document what you had to exclude

**Where.** A spec plus its own config in `week4/generated/`.

**Constraints — these are the exercise:**

- **No `maxDiffPixelRatio` above 0.05.** Loosening the threshold until it passes is not a fix.
- **No `waitForTimeout`** as the stability mechanism
- Ten consecutive green runs (`--repeat-each=10`)

Then answer in a comment: *after everything you excluded, is this test still worth having?*

**Check yourself.** Ten green runs. Then re-read your exclusions — if you masked most of the page, the
honest answer is "no", and saying so is the right outcome.

> **Hint** — this is the problem where "don't write this test" may be the correct engineering answer.
